headline: Lebanon gets ten days of peace while Myanmar cuts Aung San Suu Kyi's sentence in half.
subheadline: When dictatorships offer mercy and democracies broker truces, someone is preparing for worse things.
editorialBody: Ben Roberts-Smith got bail in Australia today while facing war crimes charges for what he allegedly did in Afghanistan. The former SAS soldier, once Australia's most decorated living veteran, is now out on bail while prosecutors build their case around dead civilians and a culture of impunity that ran from Kabul to Canberra. The irony writes itself: a man who may have committed atrocities in the name of bringing justice to Afghanistan walks free in the country that sent him there.

Meanwhile, Myanmar's junta just cut Aung San Suu Kyi's prison sentence by four and a half years as part of a "broad-ranging amnesty deal," according to SCMP reporting. The Nobel Peace Prize winner, who spent decades under house arrest fighting for democracy only to preside over genocide against the Rohingya, now gets a slightly shorter sentence from the generals who overthrew her. Everyone's hands are dirty in Myanmar's tragedy, but the junta's sudden mercy suggests they need something from the international community. Probably money.

The day's most consequential news broke in the Middle East, where Israel and Lebanon agreed to a ten-day ceasefire according to Bloomberg. Yet Middle East Eye reports Israel is already carrying out "massive" demolitions in south Lebanon despite the truce, while Macron warns the ceasefire is "already undermined." Tens of thousands are returning to southern Lebanon anyway, because home is home even when it's rubble. The ceasefire will hold exactly as long as both sides need it to, which appears to be about as long as it takes to reload.

Asian markets fell on the fragile nature of Middle East peace, per CNBC, with sentiment scores reflecting the contradiction: Conflict & Security sits at a neutral 54/100 while the broader global sentiment reads optimistic at 61/100. The algorithms see ceasefires as good news until they remember what ceasefires usually precede.

Bitcoin sentiment remains bullish at 70/100, seemingly unbothered by geopolitical chaos, though its market signal reads a more cautious 50. Crypto has learned to ignore everything except Federal Reserve policy and Elon Musk tweets, which may be the most rational response to current events available.

In quieter corners of the world's machinery, Vietnamese airlines agreed to lease up to 10 C909 jets from Chinese manufacturers, another small victory for Beijing's campaign to break Boeing and Airbus duopoly. Hong Kong flagged oil tankers are testing US blockades in the Strait of Hormuz. The global supply chains that make modern life possible continue their delicate dance around sanctions, tariffs, and the threat of actual war.

The day's strangest story belongs to DW News coverage claiming Trump takes credit for "Pope Leo's election" — a pontiff who doesn't exist, suggesting either a massive editorial error or the kind of alternative timeline thinking that has become disturbingly common in political discourse. Either way, it made the video picks, which tells you something about our information ecosystem.

Tomorrow brings more of the same controlled chaos: ceasefires that aren't, amnesties that come with conditions, and war crimes defendants getting bail while their victims stay dead. The machinery of justice grinds slowly, but the machinery of violence runs on Swiss time.
